extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and literary critics (practitioners of dramatic poetry and theatrical criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for judging or composing dramatic poetry (plays) with emphasis on language, wit, conformity to contemporary taste, and artistic advancement versus merely relying on antiquity. Intended to guide playwrights and critics in assessing quality and refinement of stage works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to the age
rubrics_metrics.description: They, who have best succeeded on the stage, Have still conformed their genius to their age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful dramatist adapts their style to the tastes, wit, and conversational habits of their contemporary audience. Example: Jonson's mechanical humour matched a duller age; what pleased then will not necessarily please a more refined later age. Writing should reflect current manners and sensibilities rather than slavishly imitate the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of wit, language, and conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: "An improvement of our Wit, Language and Conversation; or, an alteration in them for the better."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central desirable quality is refinement—clearer, more proper, and more tasteful expression of wit and everyday speech. Plays should embody improvements in linguistic and conversational norms so that the drama benefits from the greater refinement of the age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language refinement: reject improper old words or admit better new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement principally consists either in rejecting such old words, or phrases, which are ill sounding, or improper; or in admitting new, which are more proper, more sounding, and more significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical linguistic standards: remove antiquated or improper words/phrases and accept useful new terms that better convey meaning and sound. The aim is to improve clarity and force of expression; refinement is not mere novelty but suitability and improved expressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid solecisms and flaws in sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Any man who reads those excellent poets, and compares their language with what is now written, will see ... in every page either some solecism of speech, or some notorious flaw in sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully avoid grammatical solecisms and logical/semantic flaws. The essay uses Shakespeare and Fletcher as examples where such faults exist; pointing out errors is part of improving the art. Precision of expression and correctness of sense are required because critics now scrutinize each line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiquity is not proof of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiquity alone is no plea for the excellency of a poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept earlier works as superior merely because they are old. Critical evaluation should consider whether newer writing legitimately improves on the past; an age may legitimately claim advantages of knowledge and refinement over predecessors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for contemporary critical scrutiny (care with each line)
rubrics_metrics.description: When critics weigh Each line, and every word, throughout a play, None of them, no not Jonson in his height, Could pass, without allowing grains for weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given modern critics' close reading, authors should pare unnecessary verses, attend to every line and word, and avoid complacency. Plays must withstand meticulous critical judgment; economy and deliberateness in wording are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to advance the art (do not let poetry regress)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have no other ambition in this essay, than that poetry may not go backward, when all other arts and sciences are advancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The playwright's goal should be to contribute positively to the progression of dramatic poetry—adopt improvements in language and technique and avoid repeating past faults. Artistic development is a duty, not merely preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match comedic tone to contemporary manners (avoid coarse/mechanical humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Then comedy was faultless, but 'twas coarse: Cobb's tankard was a jest, and Otter's horse. And, as their comedy, their love was mean; Except, by chance, in some one laboured scene, Which must atone for an ill-written play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy that relied on coarse, mechanical jokes fitted a past age when conversation was less refined; in a more polished age, such humour feels outdated. Comedic devices and subject-matter should suit the audience's current level of wit; isolated excellent scenes may not redeem an otherwise ill-written play.
